core.text: 2. Related Work
2.1. Interactive Learning from Human Feedback

Learning from Demonstration (LfD) aims to learn a policy by imitating expert actions (Pomerleau, 1988). The three main challenges are 1) the distribution shift due to error accumulation (Osa et al., 2018), 2) causal confusion where the policy is conditioned on task-irrelevant features (De Haan et al., 2019), and 3) imperfect demonstrations from the demonstrators (Wu et al., 2019).

Previous attempts have explored an interactive teaching paradigm in which the human teacher iteratively refines the learned policy. This includes trajectory relabeling (Ross et al., 2011) with shared autonomy (Luo et al., 2025) to reduce human input, imperfection-aware learning algorithms that detect and adjust when the human teacher is not paying attention or giving incorrect feedback (Kessler Faulkner and Thomaz, 2021; Faulkner and Thomaz, 2023), and incorporating various types of feedback (Fitzgerald et al., 2022) for more efficient human queries. Others have replaced the human teacher with an LLM (Wang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025).

Our work is the most similar to (Peng et al., 2024) where we used LLMs to incorporate semantic information. But ours allows the instruction-guided policy structure generation in addition to feature engineering. Compared to previous work on structured policies (Zhu et al., 2025), we formulate the agent learning process as an interactive process, where demonstrators do not have to get everything right the first time and can continue to inspect what the agent has learned.
2.2. Complementing Learning with Language

Given recent advancements in language encoders (Wei et al., 2022a) and multimodal alignment (Driess et al., 2023), much work has explored how language can be used to augment learning in continuous embodied domains.

Several works have looked at aligning language with task specifications to leverage similarities between tasks (Lynch and Sermanet, 2021; Yu and Mooney, 2022), failure trajectory to learn error recovery (Dai et al., 2025), and action primitives to take user corrections on the fly (Shi et al., 2024). Other works involve expressing actions in language and exploiting the zero-shot capabilities of LLMs to output low-level commands in language-like coding (Tang et al., 2023). Many recent works explored the use of LLMs’ coding capability to convert language commands into code for reward design in learning (Ma et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025), robot plans (Liang et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023), and policy structures (Zhu et al., 2025).

Our work also follows the language-to-structure generation paradigm for a more efficient interpretation of the demonstrations. However, instead of relying on long and specific domain knowledge from experts or environment definition, it is designed to take instructions from laypeople who may have general knowledge for the task but could not fully specify all aspects of the policy.
2.3. Interactive Learning with Code Generation

To convert the users’ needs to robot policies, many works have investigated how to make programming AI agents more accessible. Some work has designed interfaces for laypeople to specify an RL problem by defining goal conditions using graphical programming (Zhao et al., 2022; Ayalew et al., 2025), designing finite state machines from instructions (Gan et al., 2024), and injecting constraints into tabular-based policies (Brawer et al., 2023). Others utilize program synthesis on a predefined syntax for web application automation (Dong et al., 2022) or long-horizon robot planning (Laird et al., 2017; Patton et al., 2024).

Ours is the most similar to (Kim et al., 2025), where the policy is neuro-symbolic with the symbolic part generated from instructions and specific numeric parameters learned from demonstrations. We use the PyTorch library and allow the synthesized program to be any differentiable function. This gives the user more flexibility and thus can be applied not only to high-level action primitives but also to low-level, high-frequency continuous control tasks.
3. InterPReT: Interactive Learning from Both Demonstrations and Instructions
3.1. Preliminary: Structured Policy

We build on previous work on structured policy (Zhu et al., 2025). To reduce computation cost and keep the latency low, we use a variant that only uses differentiable operators, such that we do not need to perform grid search on the non-gradient parameters during training.
Mathematically, a structured policy is a 4-tuple ⟨V,P,E,Θ⟩\langle V,P,E,\Theta\rangle representing a weighted directed acyclic bipartite graph where

VV is a set of nodes that each represents a feature (observed, latent, or action) that is part of the policy decision-making process. They have semantic meanings and represent concepts (e.g., “target speed").
PP is a set of nodes that represents differentiable operations instances (e.g., linear combination or a constant).
E:{⟨ui,vi⟩∈V×P∪P×V}E:\{\langle u_{i},v_{i}\rangle\in V\times P\cup P\times V\} is a set of edges that represents how variables are causally connected through operators.
Θ:E→ℝ\Theta:E\to\mathbb{R} is a set of weights associated with each edge.

Typically, the structure is sparse (i.e., |E||E| is linear to |V||V|) since only variables that are causally related will be connected. This takes advantage of the sparsity in many tasks (Mao et al., 2023), has fewer parameters to optimize, and is less susceptible to causal confusion (De Haan et al., 2019). An example structure for maintaining a constant speed is shown in Figure 2. Note that both the observation space OO and the action space AA are subsets of VV. To simplify the notation, we use ⟦α⟧:=⟨V,P,E⟩\llbracket\alpha\rrbracket\vcentcolon=\langle V,P,E\rangle to denote the structure of the policy.

During inference time, we first assign the values of the observed features in the observation oo, then iteratively compute the value assignment of each feature node and operator along the edges. Specifically, the out (head) value of each edge e=(x,y)∈Ee=(x,y)\in E is
(1) eout=Θe⋅xoute_{\text{out}}=\Theta_{e}\cdot x_{\text{out}}
Each non-constant operator p∈Pp\in P takes in the values of the edges that go into it and applies its operation on them:
(2) pout=p⁡(e1o​u​t,e2o​u​t,⋯)​, where ​ei∈{(x,y)∈E∣y=p}p_{\text{out}}=p({e_{1}}_{out},{e_{2}}_{out},\cdots)\text{, where }e_{i}\in\{(x,y)\in E\mid y=p\}
Each non-observed feature v∈V∖Ov\in V\setminus O has exactly one edge that goes into it eve_{v} and its value is the same as that edge’s head value
(3) vout=evoutv_{\text{out}}={e_{v}}_{\text{out}}
When all feature nodes in AA have an assigned value, they will be reconstructed into the action vector a^\hat{a}. We denote this process as
(4) a^:=π⟨⟦α⟧,Θ⟩​(s)\hat{a}\vcentcolon=\pi_{\langle\llbracket\alpha\rrbracket,\Theta\rangle}(s)

In practice, a structured policy is implemented as a PyTorch model (Paszke et al., 2019) where the compute graph represents the structure and parameter updates through gradient descent are easily achievable.
3.2. Agent

Formally, each agent instance is a 44-tuple 𝒜i=⟨ℐi,𝒟i,⟦α⟧i,Θi⟩\mathcal{A}_{i}=\langle\mathcal{I}_{i},\mathcal{D}_{i},\llbracket\alpha\rrbracket_{i},\Theta_{i}\rangle, where ℐ\mathcal{I} is the current set of instructions (e.g., “slow down before turns"), 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the current set of demonstrations, and ⟦α⟧i\llbracket\alpha\rrbracket_{i} is as defined above for the policy structure.
3.3. Policy Training
Given a structure ⟦α⟧i\llbracket\alpha\rrbracket_{i} and a set of demonstrations 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i}, we can train the weights using the standard imitation learning objective (Pomerleau, 1988):

3.4. Policy Restructuring

Given a set of instructions ℐi\mathcal{I}_{i}, we want to generate a policy structure ⟦α⟧i\llbracket\alpha\rrbracket_{i} that follows the instructions and performs well in the task domain. As it is likely that a layperson would not fully specify all the details of the policy structure, we rely on the existing world knowledge in LLMs to make sensible design choices. Essentially, the structure will be based primarily on the instructions ℐi\mathcal{I}_{i}, but the LLM is expected to fill in with its own knowledge and use its coding capability to translate it into an executable model.

To accommodate diverse instructions from laypeople, we increase robustness using chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022b) and in-context learning (Dong et al., 2024). Specifically, the LLM is provided with an example of an instruction-model pair (ℐLander,⟦α⟧Lander\mathcal{I}_{\text{Lander}},\llbracket\alpha\rrbracket_{\text{Lander}}) in a completely different task of Lunar Lander (Towers et al., 2024). This makes use of the few-shot learning capability of LLMs and is expected to generate responses that follow the instruction better (Liu et al., 2024). The chain-of-thought prompting instructs the LLM to do the following steps:
Extract all relevant features from the instructions. This formalizes VV in the policy structure, resulting in a list of variable names and shapes such as

Describe the structure in an English paragraph. The generated paragraph adds filler content to the instructions. For example, the instruction might say only “try to stay in the middle of the road", and the LLM needs to complete the components on how that translates into the action of steering. For instance, from the instruction above, the LLM generates:

“The policy computes summaries of the upcoming tiles (mean lateral offset and mean relative heading, …). It builds a raw steering command as a linear combination of these summaries and the car’s current heading. …”
Plan all the connections and operations. This formalizes PP and EE in the policy structure.
Generate the PyTorch model by assembling all components. The generated model is executable and reflects the instructions. An example is shown in Listing 1.
Having an intermediate step describing the structure in English has been empirically shown to improve the quality of the generation (Zhu and Simmons, 2024). Therefore, the query process is

Where ++ is message concatenation and 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the system prompt that explains the input and output format to LLM, chain-of-thought steps, task-agnostic specifications such as the differentiability constraints, etc.
Upon receiving a new instruction II, the agent is updated with

3.5. Strategy Summary and Rollouts

During the structure generation process, an English description of the structure is already generated as an intermediate step, and it is closely tied to the generated PyTorch model. Therefore, we can directly display it as a summary of the agent strategy. The summary only reflects the structure of the policy along with some constants. It gives the user an idea of what features are being considered for which aspects of the task and how they are being connected.

For rolling out the policy, the user can pick whatever starting configuration they are interested in, and the agent deterministically selects an action based on its policy π⟨⟦α⟧,Θ⟩\pi_{\langle\llbracket\alpha\rrbracket,\Theta\rangle} and keeps choosing actions based on the new observation received. This process demonstrates the overall behavior of the agent.
4. User Study

To verify the efficacy of InterPReT among end-users without much technical background in policy training, we conducted an in-person between-subject user study with 34 users. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of our institution.
4.1. Setup

We use the car racing environment (Figure 3) in the gymnasium package (Towers et al., 2024) for our experiment. The task is chosen for two main reasons: 1) driving is a common task with which most people have prior knowledge, and 2) driving well on an unfamiliar simulator is hard for most laypeople, which reflects the challenge of giving optimal demonstrations in many real-world tasks.

We use a structured representation of the environment for the policy, where the observations consist of the current speed and heading of the egocentric race car and information about a fixed number of tiles in front of the race car (orientation, lateral distance, etc.). The action space is the continuous control of the steering, gas pedal, and brake pedal. The human participants see an image rendering of the environment and give demonstrations using a gamepad controller for continuous action inputs.

The main objective of the car racing task is to finish the track as quickly as possible. The metric we use throughout the study is the effective average speed given a time cutoff tcutofft_{\text{cutoff}}
(14) E​A​Stcutoff=min⁡(Ntotal,Ncutoff)min⁡(ttotal,tcutoff)EAS_{t_{\text{cutoff}}}=\dfrac{\min(N_{\text{total}},N_{\text{cutoff}})}{\min(t_{\text{total}},t_{\text{cutoff}})}

Where tcutofft_{\text{cutoff}} is the maximum time for the policy to run, ttotalt_{\text{total}} is the total time used to complete the entire track, NcutoffN_{\text{cutoff}} is the number of tiles covered before the cutoff time, and NtotalN_{\text{total}} is the total number of tiles on the track. Consistent with the default setting (Towers et al., 2024), we use tcutoff=1000t_{\text{cutoff}}=1000 steps (40​s40s) and Ntotal=1000N_{\text{total}}=1000. We will use “Average Speed" (A​SAS) to represent E​A​S1000EAS_{1000} for the rest of the paper.

The study has two conditions: 1) the experimental condition, where participants are allowed to give instructions in addition to demonstrations and the model is trained with InterPReT, and 2) the baseline condition, where participants provide only demonstrations and the policy is represented by a multilayer perceptron (MLP) (Haykin, 1994). In both cases, the policy is trained with the same training configuration (learning rate, batch size, etc.)
4.2. Study Protocol

3939 participants were recruited through flyers and a posting in a designated research participants pool. 44 of the participants did not complete the study for personal or model-unrelated technical reasons, and 11 participant was removed as their performance deviated more than three standard deviations from the general mean among all participants (N=34,M=49.303,S​D=13.581N=34,M=49.303,SD=13.581). The removed participant had an average speed of 7.2887.288, and their trained policy was worse than a constant policy that only steered left (average speed 7.6887.688). There are 1919 female participants and 1515 male participants, ranging from 1818 to 4444 years of age. 2929 out of 3434 participants reported “minimal or no experience in developing AI algorithms".

Upon arrival, participants were instructed to fill out a consent form and a background survey before starting the study. Then a practice interface was shown to get them acquainted with controlling the race car with the gamepad controller. In this stage, the track layouts are randomized so that the participant can practice general driving with the controller instead of overfitting to a specific track. The participant had to cover 90%90\% of the track and achieve an average speed of 4242 to pass a lap. They had to pass 33 laps consecutively to pass the practice session or attempt it 2020 times before they could move on. This process took around 44 minutes, on average, with a standard deviation of 3 minutes.

After practicing, the participants moved on to teaching the agent to drive. The same track layout was used for both giving demonstrations and evaluating the learned policy’s performance. The participant could choose the initial position, orientation, and speed of the race car if they wanted to increase the diversity of their demonstrations or to see how well the learned policy performed under different conditions. This allowed participants to give targeted demonstrations similar to DAgger (Ross et al., 2011). During the study, we found that some participants took advantage of this setup and gave multiple individual demonstrations on different segments of the track because they were unable to reliably finish the entire track.

Participants were allowed to provide as many demonstrations (and instructions under the experimental condition) as they wanted, and there was no limit on the number of policies that they could train. They could also test their trained agent with any starting configuration on the track for unlimited times. However, they were required to test it at least four times to thoroughly evaluate their agent before stopping teaching. To incentivize participants to try their best to train policies, we provided up to $5\$5 performance-based bonus, in addition to the $15\$15 base compensation, which depended on the average speed of their learned policy starting from rest and at an unknown position on the same track. On average, participants received $18\$18 total compensation for both conditions.

After the participants submitted their final policy, they were instructed to complete a survey on system usability (Brooke and others, 1996), the expectation of how the agent performs on different tracks, and some qualitative feedback on their experience. During that time, their agent was automatically evaluated to determine their compensation. At the end of the study, the participant was debriefed.
4.3. Hypotheses
We hypothesize that having an instruction-instantiated structured policy helps to interpret demonstrations more effectively. Therefore,
H1: InterPReT needs fewer demonstrations to achieve similar performance;
Furthermore, we hypothesize that given the structured policy space, InterPReT is more robust to different use cases beyond the ones that the participants trained in than the baseline. Specifically,
H2: InterPReT performs better on unseen tracks;
H3: InterPReT performs better in edge cases starting configurations on the seen training track;
H4: InterPReT performs better on the seen training track with action noise;
Also, we collect user’s perceived performance to complement the single-factored quantitative evaluation. As the instructions complement potentially imperfect demonstrations, we hypothesize that
H5: Users perceive InterPReT to perform better than them;
Finally, since most laypeople can think of some general instruction for driving easily, we hypothesize that
H6: The usability of InterPReT is no worse than the baseline.
5. Quantitative Results
5.1. Data Usage for Training

Figure 4 shows the average speed of the trained policies in nominal configuration (seen track, no noise, starting at the center of the track with initial speed 4040). The Welch t-test (Welch, 1938) shows no evidence suggesting that the mean of InterPReT (n=17,M=51.488,S​D=11.119n=17,M=51.488,SD=11.119) differs from the baseline (n=17,M=49.591,S​D=12.364n=17,M=49.591,SD=12.364) with t⁡(31.65)=−0.470,p=0.641t(31.65)=-0.470,p=0.641. A further two one-sided test procedure (Schuirmann, 1987) indicates that the two groups are equivalent with bounds ±9\pm 9 (p=0.0439p=0.0439). This verifies that participants from both conditions have similar stopping criteria and achieve similar performance in nominal configurations.

Figure 5 shows the number of demonstrations given by the two groups to achieve that performance. The Welch t-test shows that InterPReT requires fewer demonstrations (n=17,M=5454.529,S​D=3315.882n=17,M=5454.529,SD=3315.882) than baseline (n=17,M=9699.118,S​D=6233.427n=17,M=9699.118,SD=6233.427) with significance (t⁡(24.38)=2.479,p=0.020t(24.38)=2.479,p=0.020). This supports H1 that InterPReT is more sample efficient.
5.2. Robustness of Trained Policies

To test for the final learned policies’ robustness, we took the submitted policy for each participant and evaluated them in different conditions. Specifically, the “Unseen Track" condition consisted of 1010 unseen tracks, each with 4747 starting configurations that varied the initial speed, orientation, and position of the race car; the “Seen Track, Edge Case Starts" condition consisted of 4646 edge-case starting configurations on the training track; and the “Seen Track, Noisy" condition started with a nominal initial position but introduced action noise (at 22 levels) to the policy rollout. This resulted in a table of shape N×(10⋅47+46+2)N\times(10\cdot 47+46+2).
We used a linear mixed-effect model (Lindstrom and Bates, 1988) where algorithm and condition are the main effects, and participant ID and track ID are the random effects:

where A​l​g​oAlgo is categorical with 22 values (00 for the baseline and 11 for InterPReT), C​o​n​dCond is categorical with 33 values (three evaluation conditions), β∗\beta_{*} are linear coefficients, upu_{p} is the intercept for each participant, vtv_{t} is the intercept for each track, and ϵ\epsilon is noise. This accounts for the differences in the participants’ proficiency in using the controller and the difficulty of each track. We use β31\beta_{31} to represent the coefficient of InterPReT in “Seen Track, Edge Case Starts" condition and β32\beta_{32} for InterPReT in “Seen Track, Noisy" condition.

Using the Wald test for contrasts (Wald, 1943) and Holm-Sidek correction (Šidák, 1967), the results (Figure 6) support all hypotheses H2-4: InterPReT outperforms the baseline in “Different Tracks" (contrast β^=8.096,S​E=3.196,C​I95%=[1.833,14.359],z=2.533,p=0.0113,pHolm-Sildek=0.0335\hat{\beta}=8.096,SE=3.196,CI_{95\%}=[1.833,14.359],z=2.533,p=0.0113,p_{\text{Holm-Sildek}}=0.0335), in “Same Track, Edge Case Starts" (contrast β^1+β^31=8.461,S​E=3.839,C​I95%=[0.936,15.985],z=2.204,p=0.0275,pHolm-Sildek=0.0401\hat{\beta}_{1}+\hat{\beta}_{31}=8.461,SE=3.839,CI_{95\%}=[0.936,15.985],z=2.204,p=0.0275,p_{\text{Holm-Sildek}}=0.0401), and in “Same Track, Noisy" (contrast β^1+β^32=11.027,S​E=4.788,C​I95%=[1.644,20.411],z=2.303,p=0.0212,pHolm-Sildek=0.0421\hat{\beta}_{1}+\hat{\beta}_{32}=11.027,SE=4.788,CI_{95\%}=[1.644,20.411],z=2.303,p=0.0212,p_{\text{Holm-Sildek}}=0.0421). This shows that InterPReT is significantly better than the baseline in all conditions.
5.3. User Perception

Figure 7 shows the’ perceived performance of the trained policy by the users. For the seen track, the InterPReT result is mostly positive with an outlier who rated 11, so the distribution is highly skewed and does not meet the normality assumption (Shapiro-Wilk normality test returns p=0.0019p=0.0019) Therefore, a Mann-Whitney U test is used to compare the two distributions and shows that user perception in the InterPReT condition (n=17,M=5.353,M​d​n=5.000,S​D=1.412n=17,M=5.353,Mdn=5.000,SD=1.412) is higher than baseline (n=17,M=4.294,M​d​n=5.000,S​D=1.611n=17,M=4.294,Mdn=5.000,SD=1.611) with significance (U=86.0,p=0.0393U=86.0,p=0.0393). However, for unseen tracks, users’ perception of the learned policy is similar between InterPReT (n=17,M=4.529,S​D=2.004n=17,M=4.529,SD=2.004) and baseline (n=17,M=3.941,S​D=1.952n=17,M=3.941,SD=1.952), and there is no evidence suggesting that there is a difference (t⁡(14.16)=−0.979,p=0.344t(14.16)=-0.979,p=0.344) based on a Welch t-test. This shows partial support for H5. In particular, it shows that although users recognize the better performance of policies trained by InterPReT, they cannot identify the key features that allow it to be generalized to other unseen scenarios.

A one-sided Welch t-test confirms H6: InterPReT (n=17,M=27.765,S​D=2.969n=17,M=27.765,SD=2.969) is not worse than the baseline (n=17,M=27.824,S​D=2.856n=17,M=27.824,SD=2.856) with significance (t⁡(31.95)=0.059,pone-sided=0.0235t(31.95)=0.059,p_{\text{one-sided}}=0.0235) on the system usability scale (SUS) (Brooke and others, 1996) reported by the participants (Figure 8). Additionally, no evidence suggests a difference in completion times (in minutes) between InterPReT (M=35.919,S​D=12.082M=35.919,SD=12.082) and baseline (M=28.489,S​D=14.138M=28.489,SD=14.138 minutes), t⁡(31.24)=−1.647,p=0.110t(31.24)=-1.647,p=0.110. This shows that despite having to think about and articulate some driving instructions, it did not affect the overall usability of the teaching system.
6. Analysis
6.1. Improvement through Interactions

We evaluated all the policies trained by each participant using InterPReT on the seen track at the nominal starting position (Figure 9). To test whether the improvement has statistical significance, we fit another linear mixed-effect model with the index of each trained policy as T​r​i​a​l​I​DTrialID:
(16) A​S∼β0+β1⋅T​r​i​a​l​I​D+up+ϵAS\sim\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}\cdot TrialID+u_{p}+\epsilon

The Wald test shows that InterPReT’ performance improves as the number of interactions increases (contrast β^1=1.212,S​E=0.412,\hat{\beta}_{1}=1.212,SE=0.412, C​I95%=[0.404,2.020],z=2.940,p=0.00328CI_{\text{95\%}}=[0.404,2.020],z=2.940,p=0.00328). This shows that interaction is important for policy training. Intuitively, this attributes to the users being able to give targeted demonstrations or instructions after receiving feedback from the agent.
6.2. Handling Diverse Instructions

LLMs have been shown to sometimes be very sensitive to prompt changes - minor paraphrasing of prompts may lead to drastically different outputs (Salinas and Morstatter, 2024). Therefore, it is important to investigate how robust it is in handling the diverse languages used by participants.

Figure 10 shows the distribution of the number of tokens in the instructions given by the participants. On average, each user uses 5555 tokens, which is a 90%90\% reduction from previous work that requires detailed instructions (Zhu et al., 2025). This highlights the user friendliness of InterPReT. The provided instructions cover a wide range of styles:
Terse and Abstract: “Stay within the grey track”
Terse and Specific: “Desired speed is 70.”

Verbose: “when turning prioritize the middle of the road rather than the inside of the bend. this will limit your chances of hitting grass. in general, try to stay in the middle of the road since you are surrounded by grass”
Second-person: “speed up to go as fast as you can”
Third-person: “Keep the car straight on a straight road”
Typo: “Turn a corner”
Except for a few common instructions such as “stay on the road" and “slow down at turns", most instructions appear only once.

Listing 2 shows examples of the generated models having the same latent variable representation from syntactically different instructions. This shows that InterPReT can correctly identify key latent features and is robust to variations in the expression of instructions. Meanwhile, Listing 3 shows that the generated model correctly mirrors the user’s instruction of “brake proportional to …" by using a multiplication function directly on the output action space (participant D), and it also explicitly modeled the desired speed when the instruction focuses on the speed of the car instead of a specific action (participant E). This shows that it can capture the nuances and follow the instructions closely instead of returning the same model every time.
6.3. User Leveraging Strategy Summary

We found that some participants deliberately referenced the variable names reflected in the summary of the strategy to communicate better with the model generation process. For example, after the agent displayed:
“… It [the agent] computes a desired speed that is low (25) when a sharp corner ( border=1) is close, and high (85) when no corner is near. …”
The user used the same concept of border to define straight lines in their instructions:
“Accelerate to maximum speed if the road is straight or the corner is not sharp ( border<0.4) ahead”
Which is generated as
para/tagging=false
para/tagging=true

This shows that in addition to providing inspiration for new demonstrations and instructions, the summary generated establishes a common language that is shared between the user and the agent such that the user can have direct control over the policy structure even if they have no coding experience.
6.4. Additional Ablations

In this work, language feedback and structure generation are treated as a whole as the structures are based on the language instructions. To illustrate this, we use the data collected from the InterPReT group and compare our method with two alternative formulations:
Fixed Structure (no instruction): A policy structure generated by LLM without any human instructions.
Feature-Engineered MLP (no structure): The LLM generates only a feature-engineering layer, based on user instructions, before the fully connected layers in an MLP.

Figure 11 shows the average speed per participant in each condition for InterPReT and the two alternatives. Paired Welch t-test with Holm-Sidak correction shows that InterPReT outperforms the others in all conditions (pHolm-Sildek=0.0259p_{\text{Holm-Sildek}}=0.0259 for Fixed Structure, Seen Track, Noisy; pHolm-Sildek<0.001p_{\text{Holm-Sildek}}<0.001 for the rest).

This shows that having a structured policy alone, without user instructions, is unsuitable for imitation learning, as the LLM may have modeling assumptions that misalign with the demos. Additionally, users may provide an incomplete set of features, and the unstructured policy cannot efficiently interpret the demos.
